title: Analytic and Contemporary Philosophy: The Language Turn

questions.question: Who is regarded as the father of analytic philosophy, having invented modern quantified logic?
questions.rationale: Frege created the predicate calculus and the sense/reference distinction, and pursued logicism — grounding arithmetic in logic. Russell and Wittgenstein built on his foundation.

questions.question: Russell's theory of descriptions was designed to analyse sentences like:
options: The present king of France is bald
questions.rationale: A sentence about a non-existent entity seems meaningful yet lacks a referent. Russell showed its true logical form is a conjunction of claims (existence, uniqueness, predication) — some false — dissolving the puzzle without fake objects.

questions.question: Wittgenstein's later philosophy, in the Philosophical Investigations, holds that:
options: Meaning is use — words live in language games within forms of life
Metaphysics is the queen of sciences
Every term needs a strict definition
questions.rationale: The later Wittgenstein abandoned the single logical picture: language is a family of activities, and a word's meaning is its use in a practice. The Tractatus had held the picture theory.

questions.question: The Vienna Circle's verification principle collapsed chiefly because:
options: The principle itself is neither empirically verifiable nor analytic
questions.rationale: The principle was self-refuting: by its own standard, 'only the verifiable is meaningful' is not verifiable. Quine's Two Dogmas then dismantled the analytic/synthetic distinction that survived the wreckage.

questions.question: Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions introduced the idea that science alternates between normal science and:
questions.rationale: Kuhn described science as puzzle-solving under a paradigm, punctuated by crises that overturn the paradigm itself — a revolution (Copernican, chemical, relativistic). History, not just logic, shapes science.

questions.question: Popper's criterion separating science from non-science is:
questions.rationale: Popper argued genuine science states claims that could, in principle, be refuted by evidence — conjectures at risk. Freudian psychoanalysis and astrology were his favourite pseudo-scientific foils.

questions.question: Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' is a device for:
options: Choosing principles of justice without knowing one's own place in society
questions.rationale: Behind the veil, parties ignorant of their own wealth, talents, and status would rationally choose fair principles (equal basic liberties, difference principle) — justice as fairness.

questions.question: Which thinker is the central figure of deconstruction?
questions.rationale: Derrida's deconstruction exposes how texts undermine their own claims to stable meaning. Foucault analysed knowledge/power regimes; Habermas rebuilt communicative rationality; Sartre led existentialism.

questions.question: Austin's speech-act theory distinguishes what a sentence says from:
options: What uttering it does (the illocutionary act)
questions.rationale: Austin split the locutionary (saying), illocutionary (doing — promising, warning), and perlocutionary (effecting) dimensions of speech — utterances are acts, not just statements.

questions.question: The 'hard problem' of consciousness, formulated by David Chalmers, is the problem of:
options: Explaining why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience (qualia)
questions.rationale: Easy problems explain functions (discrimination, report, control); the hard problem is why any of it feels like anything from the inside — the qualia question driving contemporary philosophy of mind and AI debates.
